ctx.x: And Dyer and Louie were friends. They knew each other. They -- I guess he must have helped her some time too, in the -- you know, happenings there. But the daughter was very nice, real sweet, and -- but she had -- at that time she told me she was inspired by a lot of trumpet players, and one in particular who had inspired me. He was with -- had been with Don Redman, different bands. Hmmm -- he's working now for the airplane company. He's working out in Jamaica -- Long Island there. Oh, what the heck is his name?…

Anyway, he had taught her, showed her a lot of things, and helped her, and she was more a modern, I would say, modern gig, because she was playing more changes, running the changes, what we -- you know what we mean by changes, the kind -- the -- uh!

items.title: 52043_Herman Autrey oral history interview
items.q: Don Redman Bradman. He played with -- what the heck, Arnold played with some of the best bands around town.

ctx.x: Very fine drummer. He was with -- Arnold played some with everybody. Wait a minute, some of the big bands, a lot of the big bands. Wait a minute. Dog-gone it, I don't know where I am. (Snaps fingers.) Some of the bigger -- Don Redman Bradman. He played with -- what the heck, Arnold played with some of the best bands around town.

Anyway, I'm -- see I'm -- I mean said where does he live? So I said I live down the street, 123rd -- 129th Street, at the end of Seventh Avenue. So he told -- I asked him if he'd like to do some records with me. Fats. I'm laying up in bed asleep with my wife, Herman! I said what? Herman! He says, hey, he says, 'how you doing? My name is Arnold, this is Bud Scripp, you know me.' I say yes, Scripp, you with Arnold Bolling.
